screens.title: Feature Envy and Move Method / Move Field
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we focus on a common design smell called Feature Envy. That happens when a method lives in one class but spends most of its time using another class's data. The result is tight coupling, weaker encapsulation, and logic that is harder to maintain. You'll learn how to identify such methods by looking for repeated getters, deep access chains, and methods that use little of their own class. Then we'll apply two practical refactorings: Move Method, which relocates a method to the class whose data it primarily uses, and Move Field, which moves instance data to the class that needs it most. You'll see concrete Python before-and-after examples using Product/DiscountCalculator and Order/OrderProcessor so you can practice safely. I'll also guide you through common pitfalls: incomplete moves, A P I breakage, and accidental circular dependencies, and show how to keep tests and compatibility intact. By the end you'll be able to choose the right home for behavior and data, improving cohesion and making your code easier to change. Ask yourself as you go: which class truly owns this behavior?

Feature Envy
Why methods that live away from their data cause trouble and how to fix them.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Practice Outcomes
Practice Outcomes
Write safe tests
Create unit tests that assert final values and printed output where applicable. Use these tests before and after refactoring to ensure behavior stays constant.
Maintain API compatibility
Consider adding a small forwarding method on the old class to call the new location while deprecating the old name if needed.

screens.title: What is Feature Envy?
screens.narratorSegment: Feature Envy is a code smell where a method in one class uses another class’s data so heavily that it effectively acts on that other class’s behalf. You typically see this as many getter calls, long access chains, or methods that barely read their own class fields. The practical definition is simple: the method spends more time and operations touching another object's internals than its own. For example, a calculator object that routinely calls multiple get methods on a product object to compute a price is a classic case. Why that matters: the method now depends on the internal layout and semantics of the other class. Change that other class and the envious method may break or need updating, increasing coupling. A helpful way to evaluate ownership is to ask: if I moved this method to the other class, would it need fewer accessors and be simpler? If yes, that method is likely misplaced. Misconceptions to avoid: not every cross-object call is envy — collaborating objects are normal; the smell arises when the balance of data usage is strongly one-sided. A correct first step is to write or update tests so behavior is protected before attempting any move. Think of Feature Envy as a signal to restore natural ownership boundaries.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › What is Feature Envy?
Feature Envy explained
Feature Envy happens when a method calls many accessors on another object and uses little of its own object's state. This imbalance signals that the method’s natural home may be the object it reaches into.
Symptoms
  • Multiple getters called on the same parameter
  • Long chains like a.get_b().get_c()
  • Method has little or no use of its own fields
Why it matters

It increases coupling and weakens encapsulation. Small changes in the data owner can break many callers, and the ownership of behavior becomes unclear.

Key Takeaway

If moving the method to the other class simplifies it and reduces getters, it probably belongs there.

Concrete example
Imagine a DiscountCalculator that calls product.get_price() and product.get_discount_percentage() and computes the final price. The calculator itself holds no relevant state. Moving the calculation into Product removes the need for those getters and restores authority to Product to manage its pricing behavior.
Analogy
It's like a worker who prefers to do repairs at the customer's house rather than bringing the item to its own workshop. The work belongs where the tools and parts live.
Check your understanding
Ask: Does the method modify or query mostly another object? Would moving it reduce the number of accessors used?

screens.title: Why Feature Envy hurts design
screens.narratorSegment: Feature Envy isn't just an aesthetic complaint; it has concrete negative effects. First, it raises coupling: when methods in Class A depend on internals of Class B, a change to B often requires changes to A. That increases the blast radius of small changes. Second, it undermines encapsulation: encapsulation says an object should manage its own state and expose behavior through interfaces. If external classes constantly manipulate B's internal data, B no longer controls its invariants. Third, maintenance becomes harder: finding where logic lives gets confusing when behavior is scattered away from the data it operates on. You will also see tests become fragile because callers must mimic internal details rather than rely on stable behavior. A common misconception is to assume many small getters are harmless; in fact, they are often a sign of misplaced behavior. The correct remedy is to move the behavior closer to the data or to create a new class if responsibilities are shared. Finally, always back refactors with tests and consider A P I compatibility to avoid breaking consumers. Think of this as restoring clear ownership boundaries so changes stay localized and predictable.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Why it hurts
Negative effects
  1. Increased coupling: callers depend on another class's internals.
  2. Broken encapsulation: the data owner loses control of its invariants.
  3. Maintenance cost: logic scattered across classes confuses readers.
  4. Fragile tests: tests must duplicate internal behavior instead of observing stable behavior.
Common mistake
Relying on many simple getters as an excuse not to move logic. Getters often expose internals that should be owned by the object itself.
Concrete scenario
Imagine OrderProcessor computing order totals by calling order.get_total_item_price(), order.get_number_of_items(), and order.get_tax_rate(). If tax rules change, both Order and OrderProcessor may need updates. Moving that calculation into Order centralizes rules and reduces the number of places to change.
Pro tip
Before moving code, write a test that asserts the final numeric result. Use that test to confirm behavior is unchanged after the refactor.
Check
Ask whether the method primarily uses its own class state or another class's state. If the latter, consider moving it.

screens.title: Move Method — step by step
screens.narratorSegment: Move Method is a deliberate, test-driven operation. Start by identifying the envious method: it calls many accessors on another object and uses little of its own state. First, create a test that captures the method's observable behavior. Then, copy the method implementation into the target class and adapt references to use self or fields on that class. Run your tests while the original method still exists. If tests pass, update callers to call the new location. Finally, remove the old method or replace it with a small forwarding method to preserve A P I compatibility. Watch out for related members: moving one method may reveal fields or helper methods that belong with it; move them too or extract a new class. Also check for potential circular dependencies; if moving a method forces two classes to mutually depend on each other, consider Extract Class or a different design. A common safe pattern is maintaining the old method as a one-line forwarder for a release cycle, then deprecating it later once clients migrate. Always keep behavior protected by tests during every step.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Move Method
Process
  1. Write tests that assert the method's external behavior.
  2. Copy the method into the target class and replace references with self.
  3. Run tests while keeping the original method in place.
  4. Update callers to the new method location.
  5. Remove or forward the old method to preserve compatibility.
Pitfall
If moving the method increases coupling or causes circular references, pause and consider extracting a new class instead.
Before (snippet)
class Product:
    def __init__(self, name, price, discount_percentage):
        self.name = name
        self.price = price
        self.discount_percentage = discount_percentage # e.g., 0.10 for 10%

class DiscountCalculator:
    def calculate_final_price(self, product: Product):
        # This method shows Feature Envy
        base_price = product.get_price()
        discount = base_price * product.get_discount_percentage()
        final_price = base_price - discount
        print(f"Calculating final price for {product.name}: {base_price} - {discount} = {final_price}")
        return final_price
After (moved)
class Product:
    def __init__(self, name, price, discount_percentage):
        self.name = name
        self.price = price
        self.discount_percentage = discount_percentage # e.g., 0.10 for 10%

    def calculate_final_price(self):
        base_price = self.price
        discount = base_price * self.discount_percentage
        final_price = base_price - discount
        print(f"Calculating final price for {self.name}: {base_price} - {discount} = {final_price}")
        return final_price

screens.title: Move Field — when state belongs elsewhere
screens.narratorSegment: Move Field is the complementary refactoring to Move Method. If a field lives in Class A but is mostly read or mutated by Class B, then the field should likely be moved to Class B. This reduces cross-class plumbing where one class must request data from another for behavior that logically belongs with the data. A typical scenario is when a utility class stores configuration or parameters that actually describe a domain object; moving those parameters into the domain object improves cohesion. Practical steps: write tests that depend on the field's observable behavior, add a new field in the target class, update code that reads or writes it to use the new location, and remove the original field. If the field is public or part of a public A P I, consider providing a forwarding accessor for a transition period. Watch for combined moves: often a Move Field is done together with Move Method, because behavior and data are tightly coupled. Also watch for derived data — if moving a field would duplicate state or violate invariants, consider computing it on demand instead. The safe path is always: test, move, update callers, run tests, and keep compatibility as needed.

keyIdea.text: Move data to the class that primarily uses it to improve cohesion and reduce unnecessary access across class boundaries.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Move Field
When to move a field
If a field is mostly used by another class, or if moving it reduces the number of accessors and simplifies logic, it should move to its primary user. Often Move Field pairs with Move Method so both data and behavior return to a single owner.
Steps
  1. Write tests for behavior dependent on the field.
  2. Add the field to the target class and migrate reads/writes.
  3. Remove the field from the original class and update callers.
  4. Run tests and provide forwarding accessors if needed.
Example
If discount_percentage lives in DiscountCalculator but Product is the obvious owner of pricing details, move discount_percentage into Product and let Product compute final prices.
Key Takeaway

Fields should live where they are used most; moving them increases cohesion and simplifies access patterns.

Safety notes
  • Consider whether the field carries unique identity or duplicates derived state.
  • Forward accessors during transition to preserve behavior.
  • Watch for data invariants; moving fields can reveal invariant responsibilities.

screens.title: Product and DiscountCalculator — before & after
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the Product and DiscountCalculator example step by step. Initially, Product stores name, price, and discount_percentage. DiscountCalculator contains calculate_final_price and calls product. get_price() and product. get_discount_percentage(), then computes and prints the final price. This is classic Feature Envy: the calculator has no state and relies entirely on Product. To refactor, write a test that asserts the computed final price for a sample product. Then copy the calculation into Product as calculate_final_price and change it so it directly reads self. price and self. discount_percentage. Run the tests with the original method still present. If everything passes, update call sites to product. calculate_final_price(), and remove the old method or replace it with one-line forwarding for compatibility. After the move, Product owns its pricing logic and DiscountCalculator may become obsolete or gain a narrower responsibility. A common misconception is that removing getters always breaks encapsulation; in this case, removing the getters and exposing behavior on Product improves encapsulation because the product now controls how its price is computed. Always run tests and consider temporary forwards if external callers need time to migrate.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Product Example
Before — original code
class Product:
    def __init__(self, name, price, discount_percentage):
        self.name = name
        self.price = price
        self.discount_percentage = discount_percentage # e.g., 0.10 for 10%

    def get_price(self):
        return self.price

    def get_discount_percentage(self):
        return self.discount_percentage

class DiscountCalculator:
    def calculate_final_price(self, product: Product):
        # This method shows Feature Envy
        # It's more interested in Product's data than its own (DiscountCalculator has no data)
        base_price = product.get_price()
        discount = base_price * product.get_discount_percentage()
        final_price = base_price - discount
        print(f"Calculating final price for {product.name}: {base_price} - {discount} = {final_price}")
        return final_price
After — moved into Product
class Product:
    def __init__(self, name, price, discount_percentage):
        self.name = name
        self.price = price
        self.discount_percentage = discount_percentage # e.g., 0.10 for 10%

    # Moved method
    def calculate_final_price(self):
        base_price = self.price
        discount = base_price * self.discount_percentage
        final_price = base_price - discount
        print(f"Calculating final price for {self.name}: {base_price} - {discount} = {final_price}")
        return final_price
After the move, callers call product.calculate_final_price() directly. DiscountCalculator may be removed if it has no other responsibilities. Tests should confirm identical output before and after the change.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Order Refactor Lab
Starter code (original)
class Order:
    def __init__(self, order_id, items, customer_address, shipping_cost_per_item=5.0):
        self.order_id = order_id
        self.items = items # List of {'name': 'item', 'price': 10.0, 'quantity': 2}
        self.customer_address = customer_address
        self.shipping_cost_per_item = shipping_cost_per_item
        self.tax_rate = 0.08 # 8% tax

    def get_total_item_price(self):
        return sum(item['price'] * item['quantity'] for item in self.items)

    def get_number_of_items(self):
        return sum(item['quantity'] for item in self.items)

    def get_tax_rate(self):
        return self.tax_rate

    def get_shipping_cost_per_item(self):
        return self.shipping_cost_per_item

class OrderProcessor:
    def calculate_final_order_total(self, order: Order):
        # This method shows Feature Envy
        total_items_price = order.get_total_item_price()
        num_items = order.get_number_of_items()
        tax_rate = order.get_tax_rate()
        shipping_cost_per_item = order.get_shipping_cost_per_item()

        shipping_total = num_items * shipping_cost_per_item
        subtotal_before_tax = total_items_price + shipping_total
        tax_amount = subtotal_before_tax * tax_rate
        final_total = subtotal_before_tax + tax_amount

        print(f"Order {order.order_id} Details:")
        print(f"  Items Subtotal: {total_items_price:.2f}")
        print(f"  Shipping Cost: {shipping_total:.2f} ({num_items} items * {shipping_cost_per_item:.2f})")
        print(f"  Subtotal (before tax): {subtotal_before_tax:.2f}")
        print(f"  Tax ({tax_rate*100}%): {tax_amount:.2f}")
        print(f"  Final Total: {final_total:.2f}")
        return final_total
Refactored hint
Copy the calculation into Order as calculate_final_order_total and replace getters with direct attributes: use self.get_total_item_price() only if other code needs it. Prefer direct computation inside the method when fields are owned by the class. Keep tests that assert numeric totals before and after the move.
Testing advice
  • Write a unit test that constructs a sample order and calls the processor method to assert the final total.
  • Run the test after the method is moved; it should pass without changes.
  • Search for all usages of the old method and update them to the new API.

screens.title: How to test and keep APIs stable
screens.narratorSegment: Tests are your safety net when moving methods and fields. Start by writing unit tests that assert final, observable outputs rather than internal calls. For numeric calculations, assert the expected total values and formatted output if printing matters. When moving a method, keep the original method temporarily as a forwarding wrapper that calls the new implementation. This preserves public APIs while clients migrate. Mark the wrapper as deprecated and communicate the change in release notes. Avoid changing public method signatures during the same release if possible. If moving a field would create circular dependencies, pause and consider extracting a new class or introducing a value object that both classes can use. For large systems, run the integration and system test suites after the refactor. If you must keep both methods for compatibility, keep one-line forwards that simply delegate to the new owner; these forwards are easier to remove later once clients update. Finally, maintain code readability: after the refactor, remove obsolete getters only if they are no longer used outside the class or if you have decided to replace them with behavior methods on the data owner.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Testing & Compatibility
Protect behavior with tests
Before moving
Add unit tests that assert the final numeric result and printed details for a representative sample. These tests will guard the refactor.
During move
Keep the old method as a one-line forwarder to the new implementation. Run tests frequently while migrating callers.
After move
Remove obsolete accessors once callers are updated. Run integration tests to find unexpected fallout.
Compatibility
If the method is part of a public API, deprecate the old name and add a clear forwarding method for a release cycle before removal.
Key Takeaway

Tests plus cautious forwarding provide a safe pathway for moving methods and fields without surprising clients.

screens.title: Pitfalls and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: When applying Move Method or Move Field, developers sometimes make avoidable mistakes. One common error is not moving enough: moving a single method while leaving closely related helpers behind can create partial and confusing homes for behavior. The remedy is to follow the trail — move related methods and fields together or consider Extract Class if responsibilities span multiple domains. Another pitfall is breaking public APIs unintentionally. To avoid this, keep a forwarding method and deprecate the old name gradually while clients migrate. Circular dependencies are dangerous: moving a method into a class that already depends on the original class can create mutual dependencies. If that happens, consider extracting a new class that both can use or redesign the interaction. A common misconception is that many getters are safe; in truth they often signal that the behavior should live with the data. Finally, misidentifying the right home is possible: if a method genuinely uses multiple classes equally, moving it to one may be wrong — consider creating a new coordinating class. The safe pattern is: test first, move with forwards if needed, and group related members to preserve invariants.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Pitfalls
Common mistakes
  • Not moving related helper methods or fields with the main method.
  • Removing or renaming public APIs without compatibility shims.
  • Creating circular dependencies by forcing a method into a class that depends on the original.
  • Moving a method that truly belongs to multiple classes instead of extracting a new class.
How to avoid them
Tests first: Protect current behavior before making changes.
Forward for safety: Keep a lightweight forwarder when moving public methods.
Group moves: Move related state and behavior together, or extract a new class.
Pro tip
If a move causes a tight coupling between two classes, you likely introduced a circular dependency — step back and consider a new abstraction.

screens.title: When not to move — alternatives
screens.narratorSegment: Moving methods and fields is powerful, but not always the right answer. If a method uses multiple classes equally or coordinates behavior across several objects, moving it to one of them can create awkward ownership and new coupling. In those cases consider Extract Class: create a new class that encapsulates the shared behavior and has a clear, single responsibility. Alternatively, introduce a value object or small domain object to hold related data so both classes can use it without reaching into each other's internals. Another approach is to add a façade or coordinator that belongs to neither original class but orchestrates their interaction. The decision should be driven by responsibility clarity: choose the design that keeps invariants in one place and avoids scattering logic. Tests and usage patterns often reveal the right direction: if multiple classes collaborate frequently around the same concept, extract the shared concept into its own class. The key is to reduce coupling and increase cohesion without forcing behavior into an unnatural home. When not to move — alternatives means if a method uses multiple classes equally, prefer extract class or new domain objects rather than forcing a move that creates awkward coupling.. In practical terms, extract class, value objects, or new abstractions when methods span multiple owners. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When to use other refactorings
Extract Class
Create a new class for responsibilities shared across multiple objects instead of forcing a method into one of them.
Value Object
Group related data into a small immutable object so multiple classes can use it without reaching into each other.
Facade / Coordinator
Introduce a neutral orchestrator to manage complex interactions without creating asymmetric ownership.
Choose the alternative that preserves invariants in a single place and reduces the need for other classes to know implementation details. Tests and usage frequency will guide which abstraction fits best.

screens.title: A safe order for refactoring
screens.narratorSegment: A recommended workflow reduces risk and keeps teams aligned. Step one is identification: find methods that call many accessors on another object or use little of their own state. Step two is to write tests that capture the current observable behavior; these tests are essential. Step three is to perform the move: copy the method to the target class and adapt it to self, or add the field to the target class. Step four is migration: update call sites to the new location while optionally keeping a forwarding method for backward compatibility. Step five is cleanup: remove unneeded getters, shrink the A P I surface, and run the full test suite. Throughout, run tests frequently and keep commits small and reversible. If you discover related responsibilities during the move, move them together or extract a new class. Communicate changes to your team and consider a deprecation period for public A P I changes. This ordered approach keeps your refactors incremental and verifiable so you can improve design with minimal disruption. A safe order for refactoring means follow a test-first, incremental workflow: identify, test, move, migrate, then clean up to preserve behavior and minimize disruption.. In practical terms, identify → test → move → migrate callers → clean up. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we focus on a common design smell called Feature Envy. That happens when a method lives in one class but spends most of its time using another class's data. The result is tight coupling, weaker encapsulation, and logic that is harder to maintain. You'll learn how to identify such methods by looking for repeated getters, deep access chains, and methods that use little of their own class. Then we'll apply two practical refactorings: Move Method, which relocates a method to the class whose data it primarily uses, and Move Field, which moves instance data to the class that needs it most. You'll see concrete Python before-and-after examples using Product/DiscountCalculator and Order/OrderProcessor so you can practice safely. I'll also guide you through common pitfalls: incomplete moves, A P I breakage, and accidental circular dependencies, and show how to keep tests and compatibility intact. By the end you'll be able to choose the right home for behavior and data, improving cohesion and making your code easier to change. Ask yourself as you go: which class truly owns this behavior?

Over the next screens you'll build four concrete skills. First, you will learn to identify Feature Envy by spotting methods that repeatedly call into another object's fields or use many accessors. I will show how these patterns look in Python and what to look for in your own code. Second, you'll explain why Feature Envy is harmful: it increases coupling and weakens encapsulation, making maintenance riskier. Understanding the consequences helps you justify refactoring to teammates. Third, you'll apply the Move Method refactoring: copying behavior into the class that owns the data, adjusting references to use self, and then removing the old implementation or leaving a forwarding method for compatibility. Fourth, you'll apply Move Field: relocating instance data to the class that owns or primarily uses it, and updating access points. Each objective includes a short mnemonic and a competency milestone so you can verify the change with tests. These skills let you keep behavior near the data it operates on, improving cohesion and future adaptability. Practice and small tests will keep your refactors safe.

Beyond recognizing and moving code, you'll practice safe refactoring techniques. I will show how to write small focused tests that assert the same observable behavior before and after a move so you can be confident the refactor didn't change semantics. You'll also learn to decide when to keep a forwarding method for backward compatibility and when to deprecate the old A P I. We'll cover how to spot related fields and methods that should move together, and how to avoid introducing circular dependencies during the reorganization. The hands-on activity walks you through refactoring an Order and an OrderProcessor: first identify the smell, then move the total calculation into Order, remove needless getters, and run tests. Finally, the assessment question helps you recognize Feature Envy in a real scenario. These practical outcomes let you refactor large codebases incrementally and safely while preserving public behavior for clients and reducing coupling over time.

Feature Envy is a code smell where a method in one class uses another class’s data so heavily that it effectively acts on that other class’s behalf. You typically see this as many getter calls, long access chains, or methods that barely read their own class fields. The practical definition is simple: the method spends more time and operations touching another object's internals than its own. For example, a calculator object that routinely calls multiple get methods on a product object to compute a price is a classic case. Why that matters: the method now depends on the internal layout and semantics of the other class. Change that other class and the envious method may break or need updating, increasing coupling. A helpful way to evaluate ownership is to ask: if I moved this method to the other class, would it need fewer accessors and be simpler? If yes, that method is likely misplaced. Misconceptions to avoid: not every cross-object call is envy — collaborating objects are normal; the smell arises when the balance of data usage is strongly one-sided. A correct first step is to write or update tests so behavior is protected before attempting any move. Think of Feature Envy as a signal to restore natural ownership boundaries.

Feature Envy isn't just an aesthetic complaint; it has concrete negative effects. First, it raises coupling: when methods in Class A depend on internals of Class B, a change to B often requires changes to A. That increases the blast radius of small changes. Second, it undermines encapsulation: encapsulation says an object should manage its own state and expose behavior through interfaces. If external classes constantly manipulate B's internal data, B no longer controls its invariants. Third, maintenance becomes harder: finding where logic lives gets confusing when behavior is scattered away from the data it operates on. You will also see tests become fragile because callers must mimic internal details rather than rely on stable behavior. A common misconception is to assume many small getters are harmless; in fact, they are often a sign of misplaced behavior. The correct remedy is to move the behavior closer to the data or to create a new class if responsibilities are shared. Finally, always back refactors with tests and consider A P I compatibility to avoid breaking consumers. Think of this as restoring clear ownership boundaries so changes stay localized and predictable.

Move Method is a deliberate, test-driven operation. Start by identifying the envious method: it calls many accessors on another object and uses little of its own state. First, create a test that captures the method's observable behavior. Then, copy the method implementation into the target class and adapt references to use self or fields on that class. Run your tests while the original method still exists. If tests pass, update callers to call the new location. Finally, remove the old method or replace it with a small forwarding method to preserve A P I compatibility. Watch out for related members: moving one method may reveal fields or helper methods that belong with it; move them too or extract a new class. Also check for potential circular dependencies; if moving a method forces two classes to mutually depend on each other, consider Extract Class or a different design. A common safe pattern is maintaining the old method as a one-line forwarder for a release cycle, then deprecating it later once clients migrate. Always keep behavior protected by tests during every step.

Move Field is the complementary refactoring to Move Method. If a field lives in Class A but is mostly read or mutated by Class B, then the field should likely be moved to Class B. This reduces cross-class plumbing where one class must request data from another for behavior that logically belongs with the data. A typical scenario is when a utility class stores configuration or parameters that actually describe a domain object; moving those parameters into the domain object improves cohesion. Practical steps: write tests that depend on the field's observable behavior, add a new field in the target class, update code that reads or writes it to use the new location, and remove the original field. If the field is public or part of a public A P I, consider providing a forwarding accessor for a transition period. Watch for combined moves: often a Move Field is done together with Move Method, because behavior and data are tightly coupled. Also watch for derived data — if moving a field would duplicate state or violate invariants, consider computing it on demand instead. The safe path is always: test, move, update callers, run tests, and keep compatibility as needed.

Let's walk through the Product and DiscountCalculator example step by step. Initially, Product stores name, price, and discount_percentage. DiscountCalculator contains calculate_final_price and calls product. get_price() and product. get_discount_percentage(), then computes and prints the final price. This is classic Feature Envy: the calculator has no state and relies entirely on Product. To refactor, write a test that asserts the computed final price for a sample product. Then copy the calculation into Product as calculate_final_price and change it so it directly reads self. price and self. discount_percentage. Run the tests with the original method still present. If everything passes, update call sites to product. calculate_final_price(), and remove the old method or replace it with one-line forwarding for compatibility. After the move, Product owns its pricing logic and DiscountCalculator may become obsolete or gain a narrower responsibility. A common misconception is that removing getters always breaks encapsulation; in this case, removing the getters and exposing behavior on Product improves encapsulation because the product now controls how its price is computed. Always run tests and consider temporary forwards if external callers need time to migrate.

In this hands-on task you will refactor OrderProcessor. calculate_final_order_total by moving the logic into Order. Start by adding a unit test that constructs an Order with items, shipping cost, and tax rate, and asserts the final total computed by the existing method. With that safety net, copy the calculation into Order as calculate_final_order_total, adjusting local variables to read self. items, self. shipping_cost_per_item, and self. tax_rate directly. Run tests: they should still pass because the test exercises the concrete result. Next, update code that used OrderProcessor. calculate_final_order_total to call order. calculate_final_order_total instead. Finally, remove or forward the original method in OrderProcessor if needed for compatibility. After the move, consider removing any get_total_item_price or get_tax_rate helper methods if they were only used by the moved logic. A common pitfall is forgetting to update shipping cost uses in other methods; search the codebase for references. When changes are large, keep a one-line forwarding method and deprecate it over a release cycle so external users can migrate smoothly. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
